Direct Connect also supports local preference BGP community tags to control the route preference of traffic on private and transit virtual interfaces.\\\\n\\\\n**Note:** AWS routers evaluate local preference BGP community tags before they evaluate the AS\\\\\\\\_PATH attribute.\\\\n\\\\nResolution\\\\n----------\",\"url\":\"https://repost.aws/knowledge-center/direct-connect-bgp-communities\"},{\"rank_order\":2,\"title\":\"How do I set up an Active/Passive Direct Connect connection to AWS?\",\"context\":\"### Influencing inbound traffic to an on-premises location from AWS\\\\n\\\\nFor an **Active/Passive** configuration of Direct Connect connections:\\\\n\\\\n* Apply the [local preference BGP community tag](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/directconnect/latest/UserGuide/routing-and-bgp.html#bgp-communities-private-transit). Set a higher preference to the advertised prefixes for the primary or active connection. Then, set a medium or lower preference for the passive connection.\\\\n* AS Path prepend using a shorter AS path on the active connection and a longer AS path on the passive connection.\\\\n* Advertise the most specific route using BGP on the active connection.\\\\n\\\\n**Note:**\\xa0AS Path prepending can\\'t be used to configure Active/Passive connections in the following scenarios:\\\\n\\\\n* Connection A (virtual interface VIF-A) is in Region 1.\\\\n* Connection B (virtual interface VIF-B) is in Region 2.\\\\n* Both virtual interfaces connect to a VPC in Region 1 using a Direct Connect gateway.\\\\n* Both virtual interfaces advertise the same prefixes with the same BGP attributes (such as AS Path and MED) on both connections from the on-premises location.\\\\n\\\\nFor these scenarios, outbound traffic from the VPC to the on-premises location prefers Connection A due to being in the same Region as the VPC. To setup Active/Passive Direct Connect connections in this scenario, apply a [local preference BGP community tag](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/directconnect/latest/UserGuide/routing-and-bgp.html#bgp-communities-private-transit). Also, you can advertise a more specific route on an active connection\",\"url\":\"https://repost.aws/knowledge-center/direct-connect-active-passive-connection\"},{\"rank_order\":3,\"title\":\"Direct Connect routing policies and BGP communities\",\"context\":\"## Private virtual interface and transit virtual interface routing policies\\\\n\\\\nIf you\\'re using AWS Direct Connect to access your private AWS resources,\\\\nyou must specify the IPv4 or IPv6 prefixes to advertise over BGP. These prefixes can be\\\\npublic or private.\\\\n\\\\nThe following outbound routing rules apply based on the prefixes advertised:\\\\n\\\\n* AWS evaluates the longest prefix length first. AWS recommends advertising\\\\n more specific routes using multiple Direct Connect virtual interfaces if the\\\\n desired routing paths are meant for active/passive connections. See Influencing Traffic over Hybrid Networks using Longest Prefix\\\\n Match for more information.\\\\n* Local preference is the BGP attribute recommended to use when desired routing\\\\n paths are meant for active/passive connections and the prefix lengths advertised\\\\n are the same. This value is set per Region to prefer Direct\\\\n Connect locations that have the same associated AWS Region using the\\\\n `7224:7200`\u2014Medium local preference community value. Where\\\\n the local Region is not associated with the Direct Connect\\\\n location, it is set to a lower value. This applies only if no local preference\\\\n community tags are assigned. {"id": "fcaf1e2f-ab3b-43ee-a925-68e9d408715f", "role": "assistant", "content": [{"text": "This comes down to BGP, since Transit Gateway itself doesn't have a "preferred path" setting — path preference is controlled by the BGP attributes you exchange over the Direct Connect virtual interfaces.

**For traffic from AWS → on-premises (outbound), in order of precedence:**

1. **Longest prefix match wins first** — if one location advertises a more specific prefix, AWS always prefers it regardless of other attributes.
2. **Local preference BGP community tags** — if prefixes are the same length, apply AWS's local preference communities to the routes advertised from each location:
   - `7224:7300` = low preference
   - `7224:7200` = medium preference
   - `7224:7100` = high preference
   
   Tag the location you want preferred with a higher value than the other. Note: if you don't set these explicitly, AWS defaults to medium preference for locations associated with the VPC's Region, and lower preference otherwise.
3. **AS_PATH length** — if prefix length and local preference are tied, shorter AS_PATH wins. You can make a location less preferred by prepending your own ASN extra times on that connection's advertisement.
4. **MED** — lowest priority, AWS doesn't recommend relying on it.

If none of these differ, AWS will **ECMP load-balance** across the locations rather than strictly preferring one.

**For traffic from on-premises → AWS (inbound to your network):** this is controlled entirely by your own router's BGP policy on the routes AWS advertises to you — same idea, just applied on your side (local preference, AS_PATH prepend on what you accept/propagate).

**Practical recipe for active/passive between two DX locations:**
- Advertise the more specific prefix only on the preferred (active) location, or
- Apply the local preference community tag (high on active, lower on passive) on routes advertised toward AWS, and
- Mirror the preference on your on-premises router for the return path.

One gotcha: if your two virtual interfaces land in different Regions but both reach the same VPC via a Direct Connect Gateway, AS_PATH prepending alone won't override the fact that AWS defaults to the connection in the same Region as the VPC — you'd need the local preference community tag in that case.

Want me to check your current Direct Connect virtual interfaces and BGP configuration to see what's actually set today?", "type": "text"}], "created_at": null}
